title: Short Stuff: Do people move in predictable directions?
summary: Short Stuff episode on whether people move in predictable directions. Josh and Chuck discuss the tendency of people in the United States, Great Britain and Japan (as mentioned) to move right when entering spaces, the counterclockwise pattern of sports fields and running bases, and how a stroke-patient and handedness studies relate to directional bias. They cover explanations including side-of-road driving habits, the clockwise convention tied to northern hemisphere sundials, wild animal migration having no geographic direction differences, architects using layout to unsettle people, and grocery stores funneling shoppers counterclockwise past impulse-buy items. The episode closes with a Philadelphia store test that funneled people left using pallets, and a sign-off.
topics: side of the road driving influence

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to directional walking
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about the show, Jack O'Brien and the Daily Zeitgeist, then introduce the topic of the direction people tend to move, especially turning right when entering stores or amusement parks in the US, and ask UK and Japan listeners which way they move.

segments.title: Right-moving bias, counterclockwise sports and handedness
segments.summary: The hosts describe how people entering a field of action tend to move counterclockwise, matching how sports like running bases and car or horse racing are done. They discuss the difference between entering a circle and taking continuous right turns, and mention studies by the Association for Psychological Science on handedness, including stroke patients who lost use of their dominant hand.

segments.title: Explanations: driving side, animal migration and clockwise origins
segments.summary: Chuck explains that the side of the road people drive on may contribute to walking-side habits, and that wild animals show no geographic differences in migration direction. He then notes that clockwise is based on northern hemisphere sundials.
topics: side of the road driving influence

segments.title: Baseball direction and architecture as a tool
segments.summary: The hosts joke about Japanese baseball running the opposite direction, then discuss how architects can steer people left in the US to create subtle discomfort or interest.

segments.title: Grocery store layout and impulse buys
segments.summary: Retail stores funnel shoppers to the right so they move counterclockwise, placing produce and essentials first and junk food and frozen items near the exit to encourage impulse buys. The hosts share personal anecdotes about pharmacies and ice cream.

segments.title: Philadelphia pallet experiment and outro
segments.summary: A store test in Philadelphia tried to funnel people left by placing pallets in their way, and shoppers crawled over them to go right. Chuck mentions Philly Strong and the hosts sign off with the show credits.
